results.corrected_extracted: The authors note a decline over time in the proportion of participants reporting a non-fatal overdose, the most substantial during 2001, and write that it is consistent with other reports of a reduction in heroin-related overdoses during this period (Wood et al., 2006, as cited) and suggests that global reductions in heroin supply may have played a role; it may also be related to the protective effect of methadone treatment and the significant expansion of methadone treatment availability in British Columbia from 1995 to 2004 (Anderson and Warren, 2004, as cited). They also note that a supervised injection facility had recently opened in Vancouver and that its impact on overdose had not yet been evaluated. Limitations: VIDUS is not a random sample, so the findings may not generalize to other populations of people who inject drugs; overdoses were self-defined by participants asked whether they had had an overdose in the past 6 months, an approach the authors say may introduce an element of subjectivity but offers advantages where polysubstance use is the norm, adding that the definitions used in previous studies also introduce limitations related to recall bias and do not provide a hard diagnosis of overdose; the exact temporal relationship between the outcome and the explanatory variables could not be ascertained, so the study does not allow a thorough investigation of causal relationships; and although it has been suggested that changing drug purity may play a role in predicting overdose (Darke et al., 1999, as cited), the authors were unable to consider it. Editors' notes: the study recorded no measure of heroin supply, availability, price or purity, so its explanation of the decline rests on the papers it cites. The letter (anchor 9) says these authors clearly point to reduced heroin supply as the reason; the paper says reduced supply may have played a role and adds methadone expansion as a possible reason. The paper it cites for the reduction in heroin-related overdoses (Wood et al., 2006, volume 101, pages 689–95, on Canadian heroin supply) is the letter's reference 3, dated 2004 there, and the study's own reference 44 (Marshall et al., 2011, pp. 1434, 1437); read since from its PDF (anchors 19 to 22), it reports fewer overdose deaths across British Columbia in 2001–03 than in 1998–2000 and fewer naloxone-requiring ambulance responses in the Downtown Eastside in fiscal 2001–02 to 2002–03 than in fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01, and measured no heroin purity.
results.note: Only the closing comparison is fixed: Wood's naloxone series compares fiscal 2001–02 to 2002–03 with fiscal 1997–98 to 2000–01, not 2001–03 with 1998–2000 (Wood, pp. 690–691). All other parts confirmed on pp. 41–44 (rendered).
